{{Short description|Shinto shrine in Okayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Okayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Okayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine main hall and worship hall|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} ===Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''South Zuishinmon'''|南随神門||}}, [[Muromachi period]], built in 1357.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2994 |title=吉備津神社南随神門|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine South Zuijinmon|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''North Zuishinmon'''|北随神門||}}, [[Sengoku period]], built in 1543.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2995 |title=吉備津神社北随神門|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine North Zuijinmon|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''Okama-den'''|御釜殿||}}, [[Edo period]], built in 1612.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2996 |title= 吉備津神社御釜殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine Okamaden|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''Komainu'''|木造獅子狛犬||}}, one pair, late [[Kamakura Period|Kamakura]] to [[Nanboku-cho period]], Located to the east and west of the Honden.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/10545 |title= 木造獅子狛犬|trans-title=Mokuzō shishi komainu|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} ==Gallery== File:吉備津神社 御釜殿.JPG|Okamaden（ICP） File:Kibitsu Jinja Corridor 03.JPG|Cloister File:吉備津神社 北随神門.JPG|North Zuijinmon（ICP） File:Kibitujinja5024.JPG|Approach and Ni-no-Torii File:吉備津神社 一の鳥居.JPG|Ichi-no-Torii ==See also== *[[List of National Treasures of Japan (shrines)]] {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Okayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Okayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine main hall and worship hall|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} ===Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''South Zuishinmon'''|南随神門||}}, [[Muromachi period]], built in 1357.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2994 |title=吉備津神社南随神門|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine South Zuijinmon|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''North Zuishinmon'''|北随神門||}}, [[Sengoku period]], built in 1543.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2995 |title=吉備津神社北随神門|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine North Zuijinmon|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''Okama-den'''|御釜殿||}}, [[Edo period]], built in 1612.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2996 |title= 吉備津神社御釜殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine Okamaden|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''Komainu'''|木造獅子狛犬||}}, one pair, late [[Kamakura Period|Kamakura]] to [[Nanboku-cho period]], Located to the east and west of the Honden.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/10545 |title= 木造獅子狛犬|trans-title=Mokuzō shishi komainu|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} ==Gallery== File:吉備津神社 御釜殿.JPG|Okamaden（ICP） File:Kibitsu Jinja Corridor 03.JPG|Cloister File:吉備津神社 北随神門.JPG|North Zuijinmon（ICP） File:Kibitujinja5024.JPG|Approach and Ni-no-Torii File:吉備津神社 一の鳥居.JPG|Ichi-no-Torii ==See also== *[[List of National Treasures of Japan (shrines)]] {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Okayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine main hall and worship hall|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} ===Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''South Zuishinmon'''|南随神門||}}, [[Muromachi period]], built in 1357.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2994 |title=吉備津神社南随神門|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine South Zuijinmon|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''North Zuishinmon'''|北随神門||}}, [[Sengoku period]], built in 1543.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2995 |title=吉備津神社北随神門|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine North Zuijinmon|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''Okama-den'''|御釜殿||}}, [[Edo period]], built in 1612.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2996 |title= 吉備津神社御釜殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine Okamaden|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''Komainu'''|木造獅子狛犬||}}, one pair, late [[Kamakura Period|Kamakura]] to [[Nanboku-cho period]], Located to the east and west of the Honden.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/10545 |title= 木造獅子狛犬|trans-title=Mokuzō shishi komainu|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} ==Gallery== File:吉備津神社 御釜殿.JPG|Okamaden（ICP） File:Kibitsu Jinja Corridor 03.JPG|Cloister File:吉備津神社 北随神門.JPG|North Zuijinmon（ICP） File:Kibitujinja5024.JPG|Approach and Ni-no-Torii File:吉備津神社 一の鳥居.JPG|Ichi-no-Torii ==See also== *[[List of National Treasures of Japan (shrines)]] *[[Ichinomiya]] *[[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)]] ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category:11]] [[Category|Kibitsu Jinja}} *[https://kibitujinja.com Official home page] {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Okayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Okayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd Rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine main hall and worship hall|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} ===Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''South {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Okayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd Rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine main hall and worship hall|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} ===Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''South Zuijinmon|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''North Zuishinmon'''|北随神門||}}, [[Sengoku period]], built in 1543.{{cite web
