Prefecture, Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd Rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine main hall and worship hall|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} ===Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''South Zuishinmon'''|南随神門||}}, [[Muromachi period]], built in 1357.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2994 |title=吉備津神社南随神門|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine South Zuijinmon|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''North Zuishinmon'''|北随神門||}}, [[Sengoku period]], built in 1543.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2995 |title=吉備津神社北随神門|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine North Zuijinmon|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''Okama-den'''|御釜殿||}}, [[Edo period]], built in 1612.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2996 |title= 吉備津神社御釜殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine Okamaden|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''Komainu'''|木造獅子狛犬||}}, one pair, late [[Kamakura Period|Kamakura]] to [[Nanboku-cho period]], Located to the east and west of the Honden.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/10545 |title= 木造獅子狛犬|trans-title=Mokuzō shishi komainu|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} ==Gallery== File:吉備津神社 御釜殿.JPG|Okamaden（ICP） File:Kibitsu Jinja Corridor 03.JPG|Cloister 吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. 吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd Rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. 吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd Rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu 吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd Rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. 吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd Rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu It is located in [[Bitchū Province]]. == Shikinaisha (式内社) == {| class="wikitable sortable" ! District !! Name !! Funding category !! Rank !! Notes !! Same as !! Co-ords !! Shrine DB |- | — || {{ill|Kibitsu Shrine (Bitchū)|lt=Kibitsu Shrine|en|Kibitsu Shrine (Bitchū)|ja|吉備津神社|commons|Category:Kibitsu Jinja|de|Kibitsu-Schrein|eu|Kibitsu santutegia|fr|Kibitsu-jinja|ko|기비쓰 신사|ru|Кибицу-дзиндзя|vi|Điện thờ Kibitsu|zh|吉備津神社|WD=Q712824}} || {{ill|Kokuhei-sha (Engishiki Jinmyocho)|WD=Q135160342|lt=Kokuhei|comment=categorized}} || {{ill|Myōjin Taisha|WD=Q9610964}} || {{ill|ichinomiya|WD=Q1656379|lt=ichinomiya}} || — || {{coord|34.670688|133.850834|display=inline}} || [https://jmapps.ne.jp/kokugakuin/det.html?data_id=183091 DB] |} {{wikidata link|Q712824}} [[sn:2]] [[sn:3]] [[sn:4]] == Accidentally Overwritten Content == {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Okayama Prefecture, Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd Rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine main hall and worship hall|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} ===Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''South Zuishinmon'''|南随神門||}}, [[Muromachi period]], built in 1357.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2994 |title=吉備津神社南随神門|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine South Zuijinmon|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''North Zuishinmon'''|北随神門||}}, [[Sengoku period]], built in 1543.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2995 |title=吉備津神社北随神門|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine North Zuijinmon|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''Okama-den'''|御釜殿||}}, [[Edo period]], built in 1612.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2996 |title= 吉備津神社御釜殿|trans-title=Kibitsu Shrine Okamaden|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} *{{nihongo|'''Komainu'''|木造獅子狛犬||}}, one pair, late [[Kamakura Period|Kamakura]] to [[Nanboku-cho period]], Located to the east and west of the Honden.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/10545 |title= 木造獅子狛犬|trans-title=Mokuzō However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd Rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. The influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen in many details of the structure.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2993 |title= 吉備津神社本殿及び拝殿|trans-title=Kibitsu dates|date=November 2019}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kibitsu Jinja
吉備津神社 | image = Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg | caption = [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] (1425), a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Okayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kibitsu Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 931 Kibitsu, Kita-ku, Okayama-shi, Okayama-ken 701-1341 | website = {{official|1=https://kibitujinja.com}} | architecture_style = | festivals = Second Sunday in May and October 15th each year | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Kibitsu Jinja'''|吉備津神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Kibitsu neighborhood of [[Kita-ku, Okayama]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' (first shrine) of former [[Bitchū Province]]. The shrine’s main festivals are held on the second Sunday in May and October 15th each year.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Overview== The Kibitsu Jinja is located in the western part of Okayama city, facing north at the northwestern foot of Mount Kibi-Nakayama (elevation 175 meters) on the border between former [[Bizen Province]] and Bitchū Province. The mountain has been worshipped as a [[sacred mountain]] from ancient times, and both the Kibitsu Jinja and [[Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Kibitsuhiko Jinja]] are located at its northeastern foot. Kibitsu Jinja was originally the general guardian of [[Kibi Province]], but due to the division of Kibi Province into three provinces, it became the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Bitchū, and ''[[bunrei]]'' from this shrine created the ''ichinomiya'' of Bizen Province (Kibitsuhiko Jinja) and [[Bingo Province]] (Kibitsu Shrine). The [[Honden]]-[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]], which was re-built by [[Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]], is a [[National Treasures of Japan|National Treasure]] and the sole exemplar of the ''[[kibitsu-zukuri]]'' style of [[Japanese architecture|architecture]], although the [[Dō (architecture)|Soshidō]] of [[Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|Hokekyō-ji]] is now believed to have been modeled thereon.{{cite web |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kibitsuzukuri.htm |title=Kibitsu-zukuri |publisher=[[Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System]] |access-date=4 May 2011}}{{cite book |title=Architectural Preservation in Japan |author=Larsen, Knut Einar |publisher=[[ICOMOS]] International Wood Committee |year=1994 |pages=121–5 |isbn=82-519-1432-9}} In addition, the three shrine buildings are designated as National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]], and a special Shinto ritual "Narukama Shinto" is famous. === Mizuko and Sorei syncretism === The Shrine has a unique dual worship of [[Sorei]] or ancestral spirits alongside [[Mizuko kuyō]]{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=239}} or cults of miscarried babies. The shrine started as a place for the Kibi clan. It has the clan's ancestors as gods. This gives the shrine a pure and protective feel. The ancestors are seen as good and helpful spirits. This is how the shrine connects with [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] means the souls of babies who died early or were not born.{{Rp|page=239}} The shrine places the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] shrine next to the ancestor shrine. It also uses running water. This setup has several meanings:{{Rp|page=239}} # The water purifies the souls of [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. [[Mizuko kuyō|Mizuko]] is linked to water.{{Rp|page=239}} # Being near the ancestor shrine suggests these souls become kind and protective spirits.{{Rp|page=239}} # As protective spirits, the [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]] guard those who remember them.{{Rp|page=239}} This way, the Kibitsu Shrine uses its ties to the Kibi clan. It creates a respectful place for [[Mizuko kuyō|mizuko]]. It links them to the shrine's ancestral and protective gods.{{Rp|page=239}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kibitsu Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto]]'''|吉備津彦命|}}, the son of [[Emperor Kōrei]] and conqueror of the [[Kingdom of Kibi]] and founder of the [[Kibi clan]] * {{nihongo|'''Mitomowake-no-mikoto'''| 御友別命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Nakatsuhiko-no-mikoto| 仲彦命|}}, descendant of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Chichihaya-hime-no-mikoto'''|千々速比売命|}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Yamato-totohimomoso-hime-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日百襲姫命 |}}, elder sister of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosasukatawake-no-mikoto'''| 日子刺肩別命|}}, elder brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hikosashikatawake-no-mikoto'''| 彦刺肩別命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Hiko same ma no mikoto'''|彦寤間命 |}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko * {{nihongo|'''Wakahiko Takekibitsu Hikono-no-mikoto'''| 倭迹迹日稚屋媛命|}}, brother of Kibitsuhiko ==History== The origins of Kibitsu Jinja are uncertain. According to the shrine's legend, it is located at the site of Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto's residence, where he died at the age of 281, and was buried on the summit of the mountain. Afterwards, the residence was turned into a shrine, possibly by his fifth generation descendent Narumi Kaya, or by [[Emperor Nintoku]], who visited [[Kibi Province]] where he built several shrines to commemorate Kibitsuhiko. However, the shrine does not appear in any historical documentation until the late [[Heian period]], until entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' dated 847 and the ''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' dated 852. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'' it was given the Rank of {{nihongo|''Myojin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the Rank of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. From the [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] through the [[Sengoku period]], was revered by the samurai, and there were frequent restorations of the shrine and donations of territory. {{Citation needed|date=November 2023}} During the [[Edo period]], the shrine's land became smaller. However, it still got a special land grant from the shogunate. This grant was for 160 koku of rice every year. There was a busy market near the shrine. People also visited teahouses and inns there. Inside the shrine area, there was a theater and a brothel. The shrine was a busy place along the [[San'yōdō|San’yodō]] for travellers. This continued until the [[Meiji Restoration]]..{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nunQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kibi+clan%22&pg=PA239 |title=Marketing the Menacing Fetus in Japan |date=2023-09-01 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-92204-4 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=282}} After the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1871, it was listed as a {{nihongo|National Shrine, 2nd Rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chusha}}, and is 1914 was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial Shrine, 2nd Rank|官幣中社|Kampei Chusha}}.{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} The shrine is a ten-minute walk from [[Kibitsu Station]] on the [[JR West]] [[Kibi Line]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===National Treasures=== *''[[Honden]]'' and ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]]'', [[Muromachi period]], built in 1390 and relocated their present locations in 1425.The main shrine has a ''Kibitsu-zukuri'' style roof, which consists of two [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''Irimoya-zukuri'']] roof are lined up in front and behind. {{otheruses|岡山県岡山市の神社|その他|吉備津神社 (曖昧さ回避)}} {{神社 |名称 = 吉備津神社 |画像 = [[File:Kibitsu Jinja 10 cropped.jpg|270px]]
本殿（国宝） |所在地 = [[岡山県]][[岡山市]][[北区 (岡山市)|北区]][[吉備津]]931 |位置 = {{ウィキ座標2段度分秒|34|40|14.4|N|133|51|2.2|E|display=inline,title}} |祭神 = [[吉備津彦命|大吉備津彦命]] |社格 = [[式内社]]（[[名神大社|名神大]]）
[[備中国]][[一宮]]
旧[[官幣中社]]
[[別表神社]] |創建 = 不詳（[[仁徳天皇]]代） |本殿 = 吉備津造[[檜皮葺]] |神体 = [[吉備の中山]]（[[神体山]]） |別名 = |札所等 = |例祭 = 5月第2日曜・[[10月19日]] |神事 = [[鳴釜神事]]（金曜以外毎日）七十五膳据神事（春・秋） |地図 = {{Location map|Japan Okayama|label=吉備津神社|position=top|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}}{{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=11|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200}}}} [[ファイル:Wachigai.svg|thumb|right|220px|社家賀陽家の家紋（輪違い紋）
（わちがい もん）]] [[File:Kibitsu Jinja -02.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|入り口の[[注連縄]]}}]] '''吉備津神社'''（きびつじんじゃ）は、[[岡山県]][[岡山市]][[北区 (岡山市)|北区]][[吉備津]]にある[[神社]]。[[式内社]]（[[名神大社]]）、[[備中国]][[一宮]]。[[近代社格制度|旧社格]]は[[官幣中社]]で、現在は[[神社本庁]]の[[別表神社]]。 『[[延喜式]]』では「吉備津彦神社（きびつひこじんじゃ）」と所載されている。[[2025年]]（[[令和]]7年）[[現在]]は'''「吉備津神社」が正式名'''である現在、備中・備後一宮は「吉備津神社」を名乗るが、備前一宮のみ「吉備津彦神社」を名乗る。。 == 概要 == 岡山市西部、[[備前国]]と[[備中国]]の境の[[吉備中山]]（標高175メートル）の北西麓に北面して鎮座する。吉備中山は古来[[神体山]]とされ、北東麓には備前国一宮・[[吉備津彦神社]]が鎮座する。当社と吉備津彦神社とも、主祭神に、当地を治めたとされる[[吉備津彦命|大吉備津彦命]]を祀り、命の一族を配祀する。 本来は[[吉備国]]の総鎮守であったが、吉備国の三国への分割により備中国の一宮とされ、分霊が備前国・[[備後国]]の一宮（備前：吉備津彦神社、備後：[[吉備津神社 (福山市)|吉備津神社]]）となったとされる。このことから備中の吉備津神社は「吉備総鎮守」「三備一宮」を名乗る{{Cite book |和書 |title=まいられぇ岡山 2016年版|publisher=[[山陽新聞社]] |year=2016 |page=54}}なお備前の吉備津彦神社側では、分霊による創建の伝承はない。。 [[足利義満]]造営とされる本殿は全国唯一の[[比翼入母屋造]]（吉備津造）で、拝殿とともに[[国宝]]に指定。また社殿3棟が国の[[重要文化財]]に指定されている。釜の鳴る音で吉凶を占う[[鳴釜神事]]でも有名である。 当地出身の政治家[[犬養毅]]は、犬養家遠祖の犬飼健命が大吉備津彦命の随神であるとして、吉備津神社を崇敬したという{{Cite web|和書|url=https://okayama-kanko.net/sightseeing/_cms/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/85ba4c00217acc9f333e2c3496cdce52.pdf|title=吉備路周遊マップ|publisher=公益社団法人おかやま観光コンベンション協会|date=|accessdate=2025-01-13|pages=9-10}}。神池の畔に犬養毅の銅像が建てられ、吉備津神社の社号標も同人の揮毫によるものである。 5月第2日曜日に春季大祭が、10月第2日曜日に秋季大祭が行われる。中でも七十五膳据神事は、御供殿から回廊を通って本殿まで75の膳を運び献供するもので、岡山県下三大祭りの1つである{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.okayama-kanko.jp/event/detail_12508.html|title=吉備津神社 大祭 七十五膳据神事|publisher=岡山県観光連盟|date=|accessdate=2025-11-15|pages=}}。 「[[ウメ]]」・「[[ツバキ]]」・「[[サクラ]]」・「[[ボタン (植物)|ボタン]]」・「[[ツツジ]]」・「[[サツキ]]」・「[[ハナショウブ]]」・「[[アジサイ]]」など花の名所でもある。また[[イチョウ]]の[[紅葉]]の名所としても知られる。 == 祭神 == 祭神は次の9柱。 ; 主祭神 :* [[吉備津彦命|大吉備津彦命]]（おおきびつひこのみこと） :*: 第7代[[孝霊天皇]]の第3[[皇子]]で、元の名を「彦五十狭芹彦命（ひこいさせりひこのみこと、五十狭芹彦命）」。[[崇神天皇]]10年、[[四道将軍]]の1人として山陽道に派遣され、弟の若日子建吉備津彦命と吉備を平定した。その子孫が吉備の[[国造]]となり、[[古代]][[豪族]]の[[吉備氏|吉備臣]]になったとされる。 ; 相殿神 :* 百田弓矢比売命（ももたゆみやひめのみこと） - 大吉備津彦命の后。 :* [[御友別命]]（みともわけのみことのみこと） - 大吉備津彦命の[[wikt:子孫|子孫]]。 :* 仲彦命（なかつひこのみこと） - 大吉備津彦命の子孫。 :* [[千千速比売命|千々速比売命]]（ちちはやひめのみこと） - 大吉備津彦命の[[姉]]。 :* [[倭迹迹日百襲姫命]]（やまとととひももそひめのみこと） - 大吉備津彦命の姉。 :* 日子刺肩別命（ひこさすかたわけのみこと） - 大吉備津彦命の[[兄]]。 :* [[倭迹迹稚屋姫命|倭迹迹日稚屋媛命]]（やまとととひわかやひめのみこと） - 大吉備津彦命の[[妹]]。 :* [[彦狭島命|彦寤間命]]（ひこさめまのみこと） - 大吉備津彦命の[[弟]]。 :* [[稚武彦命|若日子建吉備津日子命]]（わかひこたけきびつひこのみこと） - 大吉備津彦命の弟。 古くは「吉備津五所大明神」として、正宮と他の4社の5社で1つの神社を成した（他4社の祭神は後述の「[[吉備津神社#摂末社|摂末社]]」項参照）。
