=== History ===

=== Founding ===
[[File:Kibi's Nakayama (from Kibitsu Shrine).JPG|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Enshrined{{ill|lt=Kibi's Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}}}}{{small|On the far right is the pine trees on the approach. }}]]
According to the shrine's legend, the enshrined deity, Daikibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto, lived in a thatched shrine at the foot of {{ill|lt=Kibi Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}}, and was buried at the top of the mountain at the age of 281. Regarding the founding of Kibitsu Shrine, there is a theory that it was founded by {{ill|lt=Emperor Nintoku|Q313119|WD=Q313119|1=Emperor Nintoku}} to honor the achievements of Dai Kibitsuhiko no Mikoto, while a shrine legend says that it began when Kayaomi Narumi no Mikoto, the fifth-generation descendant, built a shrine in the thatched shrine and enshrined his life.<ref name="map" />

=== Outline ===
{{ill|lt=Imperial Court (Japan)|Q30253177|WD=Q30253177|lt=Imperial Court|1=Imperial Court of Japan}}, it was deeply revered, and in national history {{ill|lt=Jowa (Japan)|Q1075605|WD=Q1075605|lt=Jowa|1=Jōwa (Heian period)}} The first record is that he received the lower rank of Junior Fourth Rank (Junior Fourth Rank) in the year 14 ({{ill|lt=847|Q30354|WD=Q30354|1=847}}), and the following year he was promoted to the upper rank of Junior Fourth Rank (Junior Fourth Rank). In the second year of {{ill|lt=Ninju|Q1373077|WD=Q1373077|1=Ninju}} ({{ill|lt=852|Q30383|WD=Q30383|1=852}}), the divine rank was (Rank)|Q240268|Dignity}} Instead of Hon'i, he was given Shihon, and in {{ill|lt=10th century|Q8052|WD=Q8052|1=10th century}}, he was promoted to Ippon.

{{ill|lt=extension (era name)|Q1327274|WD=Q1327274|lt=Extended|1=Enchō}} "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" established in 5 years ({{ill|lt=927 years|Q30470|WD=Q30470|1=927}}) {{j alink|Engishiki Shinmeicho|Q11064932|Shinmeicho}}, {{ill|lt=Bichū|Q1047514|WD=Q1047514|1=Bitchū Province}}{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kayagun|1=UNKNOWN}} has "Kibitsuhiko Shrine <ref>{{ill|lt=Kogakukan University|Q1797584|WD=Q1797584|1=Kogakkan University}} Publishing Department, ``Shikinaisha Investigation Report Vol. 22 Sanyo Road'', listed as ``Meishin University'' and listed in {{ill|lt=Meishin Taisha|Q9610964|WD=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}}. </ref>.In the early {{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|WD=Q193292|1=Heian period}}, Kibitsu Shrine was given {{ill|lt=fūto|Q11458391|WD=Q11458391|1=Fūko}} by the imperial court, and the shrine area expanded by adding donated land, and eventually it was donated to the government and turned into a {{ill|lt=manor (Japan)|Q1887569|WD=Q1887569|lt=manor|1=Shōen}}<ref name="Early modern times">{{Cite journal |Japanese book |author= Hiroshi Shinomiya |title=Aspects of the Separation of Shinto and Buddhism at Kibitsu Shrine in Early Modern Times |journal= Rissho University Graduate School Annual Report |volume=39 |issue= |publisher=Rissho University Graduate School of Letters |date= |pages=33-48 |url=https://rissho.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/10438}}</ref>.

In the early {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|WD=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}}, it was donated to {{ill|lt=Ninnaji|Q1202871|WD=Q1202871|1=Ninna-ji}} and became its fief, but during the {{ill|lt=Nanbokucho period (Japan)|Q264012|WD=Q264012|lt=Nanbokucho period|1=Nanboku-chō period}}, control of Ninnaji Temple was threatened due to conflicts<ref name="Early modern" />. Furthermore, after the {{ill|lt=Onin War|Q385676|WD=Q385676|1=Ōnin War}}, shrine territory was sometimes controlled by the {{ill|lt=Hosokawa clan|Q2736120|WD=Q2736120|1=Hosokawa clan}}, the protector of Bicchu Province, and the Matsuda clan, a local power.<ref name="Early Modern Period" />At the end of the {{ill|lt=Sengoku period (Japan)|Q204023|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}, the power of the {{ill|lt=Mori clan|Q914637|WD=Q914637|1=Mōri clan}} came to power, and {{ill|lt=Muneharu Shimizu|Q1046032|WD=Q1046032|1=Shimizu Muneharu}} and others effectively ruled <ref name="Early modern" />. Furthermore, after the unification of the country by {{ill|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Q187550|WD=Q187550|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi}}, it became the territory of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hideie Ukita|1=UNKNOWN}} and received a donation of shrine territory<ref name="Early Modern Period" />. Furthermore, the ruling relationship with Ninna-ji Temple continued until the early modern period, and it was particularly influenced by rituals.In the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, it first came under the control of the Bicchu magistrate {{ill|lt=Masatsugu Kobori|Q11459515|WD=Q11459515|1=Kobori Masatsugu}} as a territory under the direct control of the {{ill|lt=Tokugawa clan|Q1412769|WD=Q1412769|1=Tokugawa clan}}, and then Miyauchi village, where Kibitsu Shrine is located, became the {{ill|lt=Niwase clan|Q3034514|WD=Q3034514|1=Niwase Domain}} territory.<ref name="Early modern" />. In April of Keicho 6 ({{ill|lt=1601|Q6725|WD=Q6725|1=1601}}), 160 koku were donated by {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|WD=Q171977|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, and after deducting the 60 koku of land removed from the precincts, the total was 100 koku, maintaining the stone height of the Ukita clan era<ref name="Early Modern" />. However, since the {{ill|lt=shuinjo|Q11093673|WD=Q11093673|1=shuinjō}} was simply written as ``Bicchu Imperial Palace Shinryo,'' there was a dispute between the shrine family and the shrine monks within the shrine over the destination<ref name="Early Modern Period" />. In the 3rd year of Kanbun ({{ill|lt=1663|Q7577|WD=Q7577|1=1663}}), the ruling of {{ill|lt=Temple and Shrine Bugyo|Q1036279|WD=Q1036279|1=Jisha-bugyō}} allowed shrine and family members to manage the main petition, and the red seals from 5th year of Kanbun ({{ill|lt=1665|Q7582|WD=Q7582|1=1665}}) clearly stated "Kibitsu Daimyo Shrine territory"<ref name="Early modern" />. Even after that, Buddhist facilities such as the {{ill|lt=three-storied pagoda|Q11357687|WD=Q11357687|1=Three-storied pagoda}} remained in the precincts, and monks continued to read sutras in front of the shrine<ref name="Early Modern Period" />.However, in the 14th year of Kyoho ({{ill|lt=1729|Q6952|WD=Q6952|1=1729}}), the shrine and family groups requested the temple magistrate to remove the three-storied pagoda, claiming that it was difficult to repair due to age-related deterioration and was dangerous in the event of wind, rain, or earthquakes, and the Buddhist side requested an injunction. The debate between the two leaders went beyond the pros and cons of removing the three-storied pagoda, to whether the shrine should be a syncretistic shrine of Shintoism and Buddhism, or whether the syncretism of Shintoism and Buddhism should be abolished as the only Shinto shrine.<ref name="Early Modern Period" /> The temple magistrate was the only one who did not directly judge whether it was Shinto or not, but it approved the removal of the three-storied pagoda, denied that the temple had anything to do with the shrine, and determined that the temple had no qualifications to sue. Buddhist buildings such as the three-storied pagoda have disappeared from maps of the precincts from the Kyoho period onward, and it is believed that the separation of Shinto and Buddhism was completed during this period.

After the {{ill|lt=Meiji Restoration|Q8707|WD=Q8707|1=Meiji Restoration}}, in {{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}4 ({{ill|lt=1871|Q7746|WD=Q7746|1=1871}}), it was ranked as {{ill|UNKNOWN|WD=Q134917280|lt=Kokuheichusha|1=Kokuhei Chūsha}} in the {{ill|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System|Q712534|WD=Q712534|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, and its official name was changed to the current ``Kibitsu Shrine''. In {{ill|lt=1914|Q2083|WD=Q2083|1=1914}} ({{ill|lt=Taisho|Q329174|WD=Q329174|1=Taishō era}}3), it was promoted to {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kanpei Chusha|1=UNKNOWN}}.

=== Precincts ===

=== Main shrine and worship hall ===
[[File:Kibitsu Jinja -01.jpg|thumb|400px|right|{{center|Main shrine and worship hall (national treasure)}}]]The existing main shrine and worship hall were built in the first year of {{ill|lt=Meitoku|Q1145032|WD=Q1145032|1=Meitoku}} of the {{ill|lt=Muromachi period|Q334845|WD=Q334845|1=Muromachi period}} ({{ill|lt=1390|Q6375|WD=Q6375|1=1390}}) under the orders of {{ill|lt=Emperor Gokogon|Q555465|WD=Q555465|1=Emperor Go-Kōgon}}.{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Muromachi Shogunate|1=UNKNOWN}}The third shogun Yoshimitsu Ashikaga|Q248381}} started construction and moved to {{ill|lt=Oei|Q1193078|WD=Q1193078|1=Ōei}} in 1425.<ref>[http://www.kibitujinja.com/about/honden.html Shrine official website], [http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=4 "Okayama's Cultural Properties"] (Okayama Prefecture website), [https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/195650 Cultural Heritage Online] etc. indicate that the main shrine was built in 1425 ({{ill|lt=1425|Q6283|WD=Q6283|1=1425}}). ``Weekly Asahi Encyclopedia Japan's National Treasures'' No. 29 (Asahi Shimbun, 1997) states that the main shrine was completed in the 12th year of Oei ({{ill|lt=1405|Q6124|WD=Q6124|1=1405}}), and that the temporary roof was replaced with cypress bark in the 32nd year of Oei, and the shrine was officially transferred to the shrine. </ref>. A gabled and flat worship hall is connected to the front of the main hall, which is built with a gabled gable structure. Hiyoku Irimoya-zukuri is a roof style in which two {{ill|lt=Irimoya-zukuri|Q855025|WD=Q855025|1=East Asian hip-and-gable roof}} roofs are arranged one behind the other, and is also called ``Kibitsu-zukuri.''The size of the main shrine is comparable to the main shrine of {{ill|lt=Izumo Taisha|Q696362|WD=Q696362|1=Izumo-taisha}} and {{ill|lt=Yasaka Shrine|Q692714|WD=Q692714|1=Yasaka Shrine}}, and the influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen everywhere. It is one step higher than the ground, and is built on a stucco-coated earthen platform (Kamebukuro), with a floor plan of 5 ken in the front, 7 ken in the back, and 8 ken in beam space, and the roof is {{ill|lt=cypress bark|Q90373477|WD=Q90373477|1=cypress bark roof}}. Inside, there is a closed inner hall in the center and an inner hall in front of it, surrounded by a lower middle hall, and in front of the middle hall is an even lower vermillion platform (Akenodan), which is surrounded by an even lower outer hall. In this way, it has a unique structure in which the floor height gradually increases from the outside to the inside. The upper half of the wall is surrounded by renji windows, which are rare for shrines. It is said to be the only example of {{ill|lt=Daibutsu-sama|Q3012037|WD=Q3012037|1=Daibutsuyō}} (daibutsuyo) applied to the main hall of a shrine, such as the shape of the inset wood, the bowl, and the rainbow beam.

The worship hall was built at the same time as the main shrine, with three girders (side lines) and one beam (front) with gables; the front is gabled and the back is connected to the main shrine. There are mokoshi floors on the front and sides. The roof is made of cypress bark like the main hall, but the lower floor is made of tile. These main shrines and worship halls are designated as {{ill|lt=National Treasure|Q1139795|WD=Q1139795|1=National Treasure (Japan)}}. - 283</ref><ref name="Main shrine and worship hall"/>.

=== Setsusha ===
[[File:Hongu Shrine (Kibitsu Shrine precinct shrine).JPG|right|thumb|200px|{{center|Hongu Shrine}}]]
It is said that in ancient times there were five shrine buildings and 72 subsidiary shrines. The five shrine buildings (Main Shrine, Hongu Shrine, Shingu Shrine, Naiku Shrine, and Iwayama Shrine) are collectively referred to as ``Kibitsu Gosho Daimyojin''. </ref>. {{ill|lt=2025|Q49616|WD=Q49616|1=2025}} ({{ill|lt=Reiwa|Q62609017|WD=Q62609017|1=Reiwa era}}7) Currently, Shingu Shrine and Naiku Shrine are enshrined in Hongu Shrine.
* Hongu Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: {{ill|lt=Emperor Korei|Q313041|WD=Q313041|1=Emperor Kōrei}} (7th generation. Father of Daikibitsuhiko no Mikoto).
** Shingu Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Kibi Takehiko no Mikoto (son of Wakahiko Kenkibitsu Hiko no Mikoto). Enshrined at Hongu Shrine. It was enshrined in Higashiyama in the south until the end of the Meiji period.
** Naiku Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Hyakuta Yumiya Hime no Mikoto (wife of Daikibitsuhiko no Mikoto). Enshrined at Hongu Shrine. It was originally enshrined on the mountain in the southern part of {{ill|lt=Kibi Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}}.
* Sanshagu - A collective term for the following three companies.
** Kasuga Shrine
** Daijingu Shrine
** Hachiman Shrine
* Iwayama Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Kenhikkatabetsu no Mikoto (landlord deity of Kibi Province).
* Taki Matsuri Shrine
* Ebisusha
*Soreisha Shrine
* Ichidosha
* Uga Shrine - Enshrined on the island of Kamiike.

Blade length 127.2 cm, warp 3.9 cm. Kizukuri, hermitage building. Hideyuki is a representative figure among the {{ill|lt=Osafune school|Q11653605|WD=Q11653605|1=Osafune school}} branch of swordsmiths called the Kowarari school.** Odachi Norimitsu (craft) - Made in the Muromachi period, Bun'an 3 ({{ill|lt=1446|Q6430|WD=Q6430|1=1446}}). Deposited at {{ill|lt=Okayama Prefectural Museum|Q3247162|WD=Q3247162|1=Okayama Prefectural Museum}}. {{ill|lt=1994|Q2067|WD=Q2067|1=1994}} Designated on April 5, 1994 <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=701 Odachi Norimitsu] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>. Total length 377.3 cm, blade length 226.7 cm, warp 5 cm, weight 13 kg. Hog-zukuri, round building. The largest Japanese sword in Japan during the Koto period. Although there is no evidence that it was used as a votive sword, the entire blade is hardened, the {{ill|lt=stem (sword)|Q1963918|WD=Q1963918|lt=stem|1=nakago}} is long, and the three mekugi holes are evenly spaced, indicating that it was made with actual combat in mind.
** Gyodo mask (craft) - Deposited at Okayama Prefectural Museum. {{ill|lt=1959|Q5302|WD=Q5302|1=1959}} (Showa 34) Designated on March 27th <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=699 Gyodo-men] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>.** Goryeo version of All Sutras (calligraphs/scriptures) - Korean scriptures of {{ill|lt=Koryo|Q28208|WD=Q28208|1=Goryeo}}{{ill|lt=period|Q11514315|WD=Q11514315|1=Historical period}}. Designated on March 27, 1959 (Showa 34) <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=594 Goryeo version of all sutras] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>.
** Paper-backed sumi-sho renga (calligraphy/scripture) - A collection of haiku from the Horaku renga performed at Kibitsu Shrine in the 8th year of Oei ({{ill|lt=1401|Q6110|WD=Q6110|1=1401}}). Designated on March 27, 1959 (Showa 34) <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=764 Honsokusho Renga] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Cultural Properties of Okayama"). </ref>.
* Intangible folk cultural assets
** Imperial House Dance - Held on {{ill|lt=July 31st|Q2715|WD=Q2715|1=July 31}} in the Imperial Palace district of Monzen-cho. Designated on March 27, 1959. </ref>.

=== Damage ===
* {{ill|lt=2021|Q49628|WD=Q49628|1=2021}} ({{ill|lt=Reiwa|Q62609017|WD=Q62609017|1=Reiwa era}}3) From January 15th to 22nd, it was discovered that someone had made linear scratches on the pillars of the shrine's worship hall and corridor. In February of the same year, a suspect who had damaged {{ill|lt=Matsuyama Castle|Q981357|WD=Q981357|1=Matsuyama Castle (Iyo)}} and {{ill|lt=Kochi Castle|Q1012815|WD=Q1012815|1=Kōchi Castle}} was arrested for violating {{ill|lt=Cultural Properties Protection Act|Q1188502|WD=Q1188502|1=Cultural Properties Protection Law}}, and was arrested again for committing similar crimes at Kibitsu Shrine.<ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book|date=2021-02-13 |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210213122041/https://www.jiji.com/jc/article?k=2021021300375&g=soc |title=Rearrest of 47-year-old man suspected of damaging Kibitsu Shrine - Okayama Prefectural Police |website=Jiji Press|publisher=Jiji Press|accessdate=2021-02-13}} {{ja icon}}</ref>.

'''Surroundings'''
[[File:Nakayama Chausuyama Kofun, haisho.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|{{ill|lt=Nakayama Chausuyama Kofun|Q11364273|WD=Q11364273|1=Nakayama Chausuyama Kofun}}}}{{small|The Imperial Household Agency-regulated tomb of Daikibitsuhiko no Mikoto. }}]]* {{ill|lt=Nakayama of Kibi|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}}
*: Many ancient tombs and ancient ritual sites remain in Nakayama, Kibi, at the rear of the temple grounds, and it is believed that it was worshiped as {{ill|lt=Shintaiyama|Q1595289|WD=Q1595289|1=Sacred mountains}} since ancient times. At the summit of Mt. Chausu (160 meters) in the center, there is an ancient tomb believed to be the grave of Daikibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto, and at the summit of the highest peak, Mt. Ryuo (northern peak, 175 meters above sea level), there is {{ill|lt=Iwaza|Q11587880|WD=Q11587880|1=Iwakura rock}}, where Kibitsuhiko Shrine is enshrined.
** {{ill|lt=Nakayama Chausuyama Tumulus|Q11364273|WD=Q11364273|1=Nakayama Chausuyama Kofun}} ​​- {{ill|lt=keyhole-shaped tumulus|Q11268718|WD=Q11268718|1=Zenpōkōenfun}} with a length of 120 meters. It has been designated by the Imperial Household Agency as the ``Grave of Great Kibitsuhiko.''
** Kibi Archaeological Museum
* {{ill|lt=Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Q500763|WD=Q500763|1=Kibitsuhiko Shrine}} - Bizen Province Ichinomiya.
* Remains of the residence of the Kayo clan - Believed to be the site of the residence of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kayō clan|1=UNKNOWN}} who served as a priest at Kibitsu Shrine. Okayama Prefecture's designated historic site <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=325 Dengayoujikan Ruins] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>.
* {{ill|lt=Myoan Eishi|Q366128|WD=Q366128|lt=Eishi|1=Eisai}}Monument of the birthplace of the monk
* {{ill|lt=Zoriyama Kofun|Q11639745|WD=Q11639745|1=Tsukuriyama Kofun (Okayama)}} - The 4th largest keyhole-shaped tumulus in Japan.

In ``{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}'' it is listed as ``Kibitsuhiko Shrine.'' {{ill|lt=2025|Q49616|WD=Q49616|1=2025}} ({{ill|lt=Reiwa|Q62609017|WD=Q62609017|1=Reiwa era}}7) {{jalink|current|Q193168} }'s formal name is 'Kibitsu Shrine''' <ref>Currently, Bicchu and Bingo Ichinomiya call themselves ``Kibitsu Shrine,'' but only Bizen Ichinomiya calls itself ``Kibitsuhiko Shrine.'' </ref>.

=== Overview ===
It faces north at the northwest foot of {{ill|lt=Kibi no Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}} (175 meters above sea level) on the border between {{ill|lt=Bizen Province|Q1047514|WD=Q1047514|1=Bitchū Province}} in the western part of Okayama City. Nakayama in Kibi has been known as {{ill|lt=Shintaiyama|Q1595289|WD=Q1595289|1=Sacred mountains}} since ancient times, and Bizen Province Ichinomiya, {{ill|lt=Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Q500763|WD=Q500763|1=Kibitsuhiko Shrine}}, is enshrined at the northeastern foot of the mountain. Both our company and Kibitsuhiko Shrine enshrine {{ill|lt=Kibitsuhiko no Mikoto|Q65318|WD=Q65318|lt=Okibitsuhiko no Mikoto|1=Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto}}, who is said to have ruled the area, as the main deity, and the clan of life is enshrined here.

Originally, it was the general guardian of {{ill|lt=Kibikuni|Q1155128|WD=Q1155128|1=Kingdom of Kibi}}, but due to the division of Kibikuni into three kingdoms, it became the Ichinomiya of Bichoku, and its branch spirit is the Ichinomiya of Bizen and {{ill|lt=Bingokuni|Q1049113|WD=Q1049113|1=Bingo Province}} (Bizen: Kibitsuhiko Shrine, Bingo: {{ill|lt=Kibitsu Shrine) (Fukuyama City)|Q6404042|WD=Q6404042|lt=Kibitsu Shrine|1=Kibitsu Shrine (Bingo)}}). For this reason, Kibitsuhiko Shrine in Bizen takes the names of ``Kibisou Chinju'' and ``Sanbi Ichinomiya''. </ref>.The main shrine, which is said to have been built {{ill|lt=Yoshimitsu Ashikaga|Q248381|WD=Q248381|1=Ashikaga Yoshimitsu}}, is the only {{ill|lt=Hiyoku-irimoya-zukuri|Q3196321|WD=Q3196321|1=Kibitsu-zukuri}} (Kibitsu-zukuri) in Japan, and is designated as a {{ill|lt=national treasure|Q1139795|WD=Q1139795|1=National Treasure (Japan)}} along with the worship hall. Additionally, three shrine buildings have been designated as national {{ill|lt=Important Cultural Properties|Q1188622|WD=Q1188622|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}. It is also famous for {{ill|lt=Narukama Shinto ritual|Q11675410|WD=Q11675410|1=narukama shinji}}, which predicts good or bad fortune by the sound of the kettle.<ref name="map" />

It is said that the local politician {{ill|lt=Tsuyoshi Inukai|Q354687|WD=Q354687|1=Inukai Tsuyoshi}} revered Kibitsu Shrine, believing that Inukai Ken-no-Mikoto, the distant ancestor of the Inukai family, was the deity of Okibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto.<ref name="map">{{Cite web|Japanese book|url=https://okayama-kanko.net/sightseeing/_cms/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/85ba4c00217acc9f333e2c349 6cdce52.pdf|title=Kibiji Tourist Map|publisher=Okayama Tourism and Convention Association|date=|accessdate=2025-01-13|pages=9-10}}</ref>. A bronze statue of Tsuyoshi Inukai was erected on the shore of Kamiike Pond, and the company name of Kibitsu Shrine was also written by Tsuyoshi Inukai.The Spring Festival is held on the second Sunday in May, and the Autumn Festival is held on the second Sunday in October. Among these, the Seventy-Five Zentai Ceremony, in which 75 tables are carried from the Gotoden through the corridor to the main shrine, is one of the three major festivals in Okayama Prefecture. 75 Zentai Shinto ritual|publisher=Okayama Prefecture Tourism Federation|date=|accessdate=2025-11-15|pages=}}</ref>.

"{{ill|lt=Plum|Q157763|WD=Q157763|1=Prunus mume}}", "{{ill|lt=Camellia|Q160121|WD=Q160121|1=Camellia japonica}}", "{{ill|lt=Sakura|Q871991|WD=Q871991|1=Cherry blossom}}", "{{ill|lt=Button (Plant)|Q163018|WD=Q163018|lt=Button|1=Paeonia × suffruticosa}}'', ``{{ill|lt=Azalea|Q189393|WD=Q189393|1=Rhododendron}}'', ``{{ill|lt=Satsuki|Q5366359|WD=Q5366359|1=Rhododendron indicum}}'', ``{{ill|lt=Hana iris|Q21558856|WD=Q21558856|1=Iris ensata var. ensata}}'', and ``{{ill|lt=Hydrangea|Q159219|WD=Q159219|1=Hydrangea macrophylla}}'', which are also famous flower spots<ref name="map" />. It is also known as a famous spot for {{ill|lt=autumn leaves|Q1156320|WD=Q1156320|1=Autumn leaf color}} in {{ill|lt=Ginkgo|Q43284|WD=Q43284|1=Ginkgo biloba}}.

=== History ===

=== Founding ===
[[File:Kibi's Nakayama (from Kibitsu Shrine).JPG|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Enshrined{{ill|lt=Kibi's Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}}}}{{small|On the far right is the pine trees on the approach. }}]]
According to the shrine's legend, the enshrined deity, Daikibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto, lived in a thatched shrine at the foot of {{ill|lt=Kibi Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}}, and was buried at the top of the mountain at the age of 281. Regarding the founding of Kibitsu Shrine, there is a theory that it was founded by {{ill|lt=Emperor Nintoku|Q313119|WD=Q313119|1=Emperor Nintoku}} to honor the achievements of Dai Kibitsuhiko no Mikoto, while a shrine legend says that it began when Kayaomi Narumi no Mikoto, the fifth-generation descendant, built a shrine in the thatched shrine and enshrined his life.<ref name="map" />

=== Outline ===
{{ill|lt=Imperial Court (Japan)|Q30253177|WD=Q30253177|lt=Imperial Court|1=Imperial Court of Japan}}, it was deeply revered, and in national history {{ill|lt=Jowa (Japan)|Q1075605|WD=Q1075605|lt=Jowa|1=Jōwa (Heian period)}} The first record is that he received the lower rank of Junior Fourth Rank (Junior Fourth Rank) in the year 14 ({{ill|lt=847|Q30354|WD=Q30354|1=847}}), and the following year he was promoted to the upper rank of Junior Fourth Rank (Junior Fourth Rank). In the second year of {{ill|lt=Ninju|Q1373077|WD=Q1373077|1=Ninju}} ({{ill|lt=852|Q30383|WD=Q30383|1=852}}), the divine rank was (Rank)|Q240268|Dignity}} Instead of Hon'i, he was given Shihon, and in {{ill|lt=10th century|Q8052|WD=Q8052|1=10th century}}, he was promoted to Ippon.

{{ill|lt=extension (era name)|Q1327274|WD=Q1327274|lt=Extended|1=Enchō}} "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" established in 5 years ({{ill|lt=927 years|Q30470|WD=Q30470|1=927}}) {{j alink|Engishiki Shinmeicho|Q11064932|Shinmeicho}}, {{ill|lt=Bichū|Q1047514|WD=Q1047514|1=Bitchū Province}}{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kayagun|1=UNKNOWN}} has "Kibitsuhiko Shrine <ref>{{ill|lt=Kogakukan University|Q1797584|WD=Q1797584|1=Kogakkan University}} Publishing Department, ``Shikinaisha Investigation Report Vol. 22 Sanyo Road'', listed as ``Meishin University'' and listed in {{ill|lt=Meishin Taisha|Q9610964|WD=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}}. </ref>.In the early {{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|WD=Q193292|1=Heian period}}, Kibitsu Shrine was given {{ill|lt=fūto|Q11458391|WD=Q11458391|1=Fūko}} by the imperial court, and the shrine area expanded by adding donated land, and eventually it was donated to the government and turned into a {{ill|lt=manor (Japan)|Q1887569|WD=Q1887569|lt=manor|1=Shōen}}<ref name="Early modern times">{{Cite journal |Japanese book |author= Hiroshi Shinomiya |title=Aspects of the Separation of Shinto and Buddhism at Kibitsu Shrine in Early Modern Times |journal= Rissho University Graduate School Annual Report |volume=39 |issue= |publisher=Rissho University Graduate School of Letters |date= |pages=33-48 |url=https://rissho.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/10438}}</ref>.

In the early {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|WD=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}}, it was donated to {{ill|lt=Ninnaji|Q1202871|WD=Q1202871|1=Ninna-ji}} and became its fief, but during the {{ill|lt=Nanbokucho period (Japan)|Q264012|WD=Q264012|lt=Nanbokucho period|1=Nanboku-chō period}}, control of Ninnaji Temple was threatened due to conflicts<ref name="Early modern" />. Furthermore, after the {{ill|lt=Onin War|Q385676|WD=Q385676|1=Ōnin War}}, shrine territory was sometimes controlled by the {{ill|lt=Hosokawa clan|Q2736120|WD=Q2736120|1=Hosokawa clan}}, the protector of Bicchu Province, and the Matsuda clan, a local power.<ref name="Early Modern Period" />At the end of the {{ill|lt=Sengoku period (Japan)|Q204023|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}, the power of the {{ill|lt=Mori clan|Q914637|WD=Q914637|1=Mōri clan}} came to power, and {{ill|lt=Muneharu Shimizu|Q1046032|WD=Q1046032|1=Shimizu Muneharu}} and others effectively ruled <ref name="Early modern" />. Furthermore, after the unification of the country by {{ill|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Q187550|WD=Q187550|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi}}, it became the territory of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hideie Ukita|1=UNKNOWN}} and received a donation of shrine territory<ref name="Early Modern Period" />. Furthermore, the ruling relationship with Ninna-ji Temple continued until the early modern period, and it was particularly influenced by rituals.In the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, it first came under the control of the Bicchu magistrate {{ill|lt=Masatsugu Kobori|Q11459515|WD=Q11459515|1=Kobori Masatsugu}} as a territory under the direct control of the {{ill|lt=Tokugawa clan|Q1412769|WD=Q1412769|1=Tokugawa clan}}, and then Miyauchi village, where Kibitsu Shrine is located, became the {{ill|lt=Niwase clan|Q3034514|WD=Q3034514|1=Niwase Domain}} territory.<ref name="Early modern" />. In April of Keicho 6 ({{ill|lt=1601|Q6725|WD=Q6725|1=1601}}), 160 koku were donated by {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|WD=Q171977|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, and after deducting the 60 koku of land removed from the precincts, the total was 100 koku, maintaining the stone height of the Ukita clan era<ref name="Early Modern" />. However, since the {{ill|lt=shuinjo|Q11093673|WD=Q11093673|1=shuinjō}} was simply written as ``Bicchu Imperial Palace Shinryo,'' there was a dispute between the shrine family and the shrine monks within the shrine over the destination<ref name="Early Modern Period" />. In the 3rd year of Kanbun ({{ill|lt=1663|Q7577|WD=Q7577|1=1663}}), the ruling of {{ill|lt=Temple and Shrine Bugyo|Q1036279|WD=Q1036279|1=Jisha-bugyō}} allowed shrine and family members to manage the main petition, and the red seals from 5th year of Kanbun ({{ill|lt=1665|Q7582|WD=Q7582|1=1665}}) clearly stated "Kibitsu Daimyo Shrine territory"<ref name="Early modern" />. Even after that, Buddhist facilities such as the {{ill|lt=three-storied pagoda|Q11357687|WD=Q11357687|1=Three-storied pagoda}} remained in the precincts, and monks continued to read sutras in front of the shrine<ref name="Early Modern Period" />.However, in the 14th year of Kyoho ({{ill|lt=1729|Q6952|WD=Q6952|1=1729}}), the shrine and family groups requested the temple magistrate to remove the three-storied pagoda, claiming that it was difficult to repair due to age-related deterioration and was dangerous in the event of wind, rain, or earthquakes, and the Buddhist side requested an injunction. The debate between the two leaders went beyond the pros and cons of removing the three-storied pagoda, to whether the shrine should be a syncretistic shrine of Shintoism and Buddhism, or whether the syncretism of Shintoism and Buddhism should be abolished as the only Shinto shrine.<ref name="Early Modern Period" /> The temple magistrate was the only one who did not directly judge whether it was Shinto or not, but it approved the removal of the three-storied pagoda, denied that the temple had anything to do with the shrine, and determined that the temple had no qualifications to sue. Buddhist buildings such as the three-storied pagoda have disappeared from maps of the precincts from the Kyoho period onward, and it is believed that the separation of Shinto and Buddhism was completed during this period.

After the {{ill|lt=Meiji Restoration|Q8707|WD=Q8707|1=Meiji Restoration}}, in {{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}4 ({{ill|lt=1871|Q7746|WD=Q7746|1=1871}}), it was ranked as {{ill|UNKNOWN|WD=Q134917280|lt=Kokuheichusha|1=Kokuhei Chūsha}} in the {{ill|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System|Q712534|WD=Q712534|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, and its official name was changed to the current ``Kibitsu Shrine''. In {{ill|lt=1914|Q2083|WD=Q2083|1=1914}} ({{ill|lt=Taisho|Q329174|WD=Q329174|1=Taishō era}}3), it was promoted to {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kanpei Chusha|1=UNKNOWN}}.

=== Precincts ===

=== Main shrine and worship hall ===
[[File:Kibitsu Jinja -01.jpg|thumb|400px|right|{{center|Main shrine and worship hall (national treasure)}}]]The existing main shrine and worship hall were built in the first year of {{ill|lt=Meitoku|Q1145032|WD=Q1145032|1=Meitoku}} of the {{ill|lt=Muromachi period|Q334845|WD=Q334845|1=Muromachi period}} ({{ill|lt=1390|Q6375|WD=Q6375|1=1390}}) under the orders of {{ill|lt=Emperor Gokogon|Q555465|WD=Q555465|1=Emperor Go-Kōgon}}.{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Muromachi Shogunate|1=UNKNOWN}}The third shogun Yoshimitsu Ashikaga|Q248381}} started construction and moved to {{ill|lt=Oei|Q1193078|WD=Q1193078|1=Ōei}} in 1425.<ref>[http://www.kibitujinja.com/about/honden.html Shrine official website], [http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=4 "Okayama's Cultural Properties"] (Okayama Prefecture website), [https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/195650 Cultural Heritage Online] etc. indicate that the main shrine was built in 1425 ({{ill|lt=1425|Q6283|WD=Q6283|1=1425}}). ``Weekly Asahi Encyclopedia Japan's National Treasures'' No. 29 (Asahi Shimbun, 1997) states that the main shrine was completed in the 12th year of Oei ({{ill|lt=1405|Q6124|WD=Q6124|1=1405}}), and that the temporary roof was replaced with cypress bark in the 32nd year of Oei, and the shrine was officially transferred to the shrine. </ref>. A gabled and flat worship hall is connected to the front of the main hall, which is built with a gabled gable structure. Hiyoku Irimoya-zukuri is a roof style in which two {{ill|lt=Irimoya-zukuri|Q855025|WD=Q855025|1=East Asian hip-and-gable roof}} roofs are arranged one behind the other, and is also called ``Kibitsu-zukuri.''The size of the main shrine is comparable to the main shrine of {{ill|lt=Izumo Taisha|Q696362|WD=Q696362|1=Izumo-taisha}} and {{ill|lt=Yasaka Shrine|Q692714|WD=Q692714|1=Yasaka Shrine}}, and the influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen everywhere. It is one step higher than the ground, and is built on a stucco-coated earthen platform (Kamebukuro), with a floor plan of 5 ken in the front, 7 ken in the back, and 8 ken in beam space, and the roof is {{ill|lt=cypress bark|Q90373477|WD=Q90373477|1=cypress bark roof}}. Inside, there is a closed inner hall in the center and an inner hall in front of it, surrounded by a lower middle hall, and in front of the middle hall is an even lower vermillion platform (Akenodan), which is surrounded by an even lower outer hall. In this way, it has a unique structure in which the floor height gradually increases from the outside to the inside. The upper half of the wall is surrounded by renji windows, which are rare for shrines. It is said to be the only example of {{ill|lt=Daibutsu-sama|Q3012037|WD=Q3012037|1=Daibutsuyō}} (daibutsuyo) applied to the main hall of a shrine, such as the shape of the inset wood, the bowl, and the rainbow beam.

The worship hall was built at the same time as the main shrine, with three girders (side lines) and one beam (front) with gables; the front is gabled and the back is connected to the main shrine. There are mokoshi floors on the front and sides. The roof is made of cypress bark like the main hall, but the lower floor is made of tile. These main shrines and worship halls are designated as {{ill|lt=National Treasure|Q1139795|WD=Q1139795|1=National Treasure (Japan)}}. - 283</ref><ref name="Main shrine and worship hall"/>.

=== Other shrine buildings ===
* Okamaden
*: {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, {{ill|lt=Keicho|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185|1=Keichō}}11 ({{ill|lt=1606|Q6747|WD=Q6747|1=1606}}) Rebuilt by miner Chitane Yasuhara. Single-story, flat-sided roof with real tiles. It is a rectangular shape extending north and south, with a cauldron placed in the north two spaces. A special ritual called "{{ill|lt=Narukama Shinji|Q11675410|WD=Q11675410|1=narukama shinji}}" is held every day except Friday. <ref name="Okamaden"/> has been designated as a national important cultural property.
* Corridor
*: It is said to have been built during {{ill|lt=Sengoku period (Japan)|Q204023|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}, between {{ill|lt=Tensho|Q1145058|WD=Q1145058|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)}} ({{ill|lt=1573|Q6678|WD=Q6678|1=1573}} - {{ill|lt=1591|Q6766|WD=Q6766|1=1591}}). Total length 398 meters. <ref name="Corridor"/> has been designated as a cultural property by Okayama Prefecture.
* Kitazuishinmon
*: Rebuilt in 11 ({{ill|lt=1542|Q6520|WD=Q6520|1=1542}}) during the Muromachi period. Single-layer gabled cypress bark roof. It was built on the approach from the front of the shrine. <ref name="Kitazuishinmon"/> has been designated as a national important cultural property.
* Minamizuishinmon*: Reconstruction in {{ill|lt=Nanbokucho period (Japan)|Q264012|WD=Q264012|lt=Nanbokucho period|1=Nanboku-chō period}}, {{ill|lt=Enbun|Q1145071|WD=Q1145071|1=Enbun}}2 ({{ill|lt=1357|Q6135|WD=Q6135|1=1357}}). The oldest Kibitsu Shrine. Single-layer gable roof with tile roof. It was built in the middle of the corridor to Hongu Shrine. <ref name="Minamizuishinmon"/> is designated as a national important cultural property.

=== Setsusha ===
[[File:Hongu Shrine (Kibitsu Shrine precinct shrine).JPG|right|thumb|200px|{{center|Hongu Shrine}}]]
It is said that in ancient times there were five shrine buildings and 72 subsidiary shrines. The five shrine buildings (Main Shrine, Hongu Shrine, Shingu Shrine, Naiku Shrine, and Iwayama Shrine) are collectively referred to as ``Kibitsu Gosho Daimyojin''. </ref>. {{ill|lt=2025|Q49616|WD=Q49616|1=2025}} ({{ill|lt=Reiwa|Q62609017|WD=Q62609017|1=Reiwa era}}7) Currently, Shingu Shrine and Naiku Shrine are enshrined in Hongu Shrine.
* Hongu Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: {{ill|lt=Emperor Korei|Q313041|WD=Q313041|1=Emperor Kōrei}} (7th generation. Father of Daikibitsuhiko no Mikoto).
** Shingu Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Kibi Takehiko no Mikoto (son of Wakahiko Kenkibitsu Hiko no Mikoto). Enshrined at Hongu Shrine. It was enshrined in Higashiyama in the south until the end of the Meiji period.
** Naiku Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Hyakuta Yumiya Hime no Mikoto (wife of Daikibitsuhiko no Mikoto). Enshrined at Hongu Shrine. It was originally enshrined on the mountain in the southern part of {{ill|lt=Kibi Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}}.
* Sanshagu - A collective term for the following three companies.
** Kasuga Shrine
** Daijingu Shrine
** Hachiman Shrine
* Iwayama Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Kenhikkatabetsu no Mikoto (landlord deity of Kibi Province).
* Taki Matsuri Shrine
* Ebisusha
*Soreisha Shrine
* Ichidosha
* Uga Shrine - Enshrined on the island of Kamiike.

=== Okayama prefecture designated cultural property ===
* Important cultural property (tangible cultural property)
** Corridor (building) - Constructed during the Sengoku period and the Tensho era ({{ill|lt=1573|Q6678|WD=Q6678|1=1573}} - {{ill|lt=1591|Q6766|WD=Q6766|1=1591}}). {{ill|lt=1976|Q2480|WD=Q2480|1=1976}} Designated on March 27, 1976. </ref>.
** Odachi inscribed by Hideyuki Osafune (craft) - Muromachi period, Choroku 3 ({{ill|lt=1459|Q6524|WD=Q6524|1=1459}}). Deposited at Okayama Prefectural Museum. {{ill|lt=1982|Q2436|WD=Q2436|1=1982}} Designated on April 9, 1982 <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=700 Odachi, inscribed Bishū Osafune Hideyuki] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>. Blade length 127.2 cm, warp 3.9 cm. Kizukuri, hermitage building. Hideyuki is a representative figure among the {{ill|lt=Osafune school|Q11653605|WD=Q11653605|1=Osafune school}} branch of swordsmiths called the Kowarari school.** Odachi Norimitsu (craft) - Made in the Muromachi period, Bun'an 3 ({{ill|lt=1446|Q6430|WD=Q6430|1=1446}}). Deposited at {{ill|lt=Okayama Prefectural Museum|Q3247162|WD=Q3247162|1=Okayama Prefectural Museum}}. {{ill|lt=1994|Q2067|WD=Q2067|1=1994}} Designated on April 5, 1994 <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=701 Odachi Norimitsu] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>. Total length 377.3 cm, blade length 226.7 cm, warp 5 cm, weight 13 kg. Hog-zukuri, round building. The largest Japanese sword in Japan during the Koto period. Although there is no evidence that it was used as a votive sword, the entire blade is hardened, the {{ill|lt=stem (sword)|Q1963918|WD=Q1963918|lt=stem|1=nakago}} is long, and the three mekugi holes are evenly spaced, indicating that it was made with actual combat in mind.

In ``{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}'' it is listed as ``Kibitsuhiko Shrine.'' {{ill|lt=2025|Q49616|WD=Q49616|1=2025}} ({{ill|lt=Reiwa|Q62609017|WD=Q62609017|1=Reiwa era}}7) {{jalink|current|Q193168} }'s formal name is 'Kibitsu Shrine''' <ref>Currently, Bicchu and Bingo Ichinomiya call themselves ``Kibitsu Shrine,'' but only Bizen Ichinomiya calls itself ``Kibitsuhiko Shrine.'' </ref>.

=== Overview ===
It faces north at the northwest foot of {{ill|lt=Kibi no Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}} (175 meters above sea level) on the border between {{ill|lt=Bizen Province|Q1047514|WD=Q1047514|1=Bitchū Province}} in the western part of Okayama City. Nakayama in Kibi has been known as {{ill|lt=Shintaiyama|Q1595289|WD=Q1595289|1=Sacred mountains}} since ancient times, and Bizen Province Ichinomiya, {{ill|lt=Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Q500763|WD=Q500763|1=Kibitsuhiko Shrine}}, is enshrined at the northeastern foot of the mountain. Both our company and Kibitsuhiko Shrine enshrine {{ill|lt=Kibitsuhiko no Mikoto|Q65318|WD=Q65318|lt=Okibitsuhiko no Mikoto|1=Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto}}, who is said to have ruled the area, as the main deity, and the clan of life is enshrined here.

Originally, it was the general guardian of {{ill|lt=Kibikuni|Q1155128|WD=Q1155128|1=Kingdom of Kibi}}, but due to the division of Kibikuni into three kingdoms, it became the Ichinomiya of Bichoku, and its branch spirit is the Ichinomiya of Bizen and {{ill|lt=Bingokuni|Q1049113|WD=Q1049113|1=Bingo Province}} (Bizen: Kibitsuhiko Shrine, Bingo: {{ill|lt=Kibitsu Shrine) (Fukuyama City)|Q6404042|WD=Q6404042|lt=Kibitsu Shrine|1=Kibitsu Shrine (Bingo)}}). For this reason, Kibitsuhiko Shrine in Bizen takes the names of ``Kibisou Chinju'' and ``Sanbi Ichinomiya''. </ref>.The main shrine, which is said to have been built {{ill|lt=Yoshimitsu Ashikaga|Q248381|WD=Q248381|1=Ashikaga Yoshimitsu}}, is the only {{ill|lt=Hiyoku-irimoya-zukuri|Q3196321|WD=Q3196321|1=Kibitsu-zukuri}} (Kibitsu-zukuri) in Japan, and is designated as a {{ill|lt=national treasure|Q1139795|WD=Q1139795|1=National Treasure (Japan)}} along with the worship hall. Additionally, three shrine buildings have been designated as national {{ill|lt=Important Cultural Properties|Q1188622|WD=Q1188622|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}. It is also famous for {{ill|lt=Narukama Shinto ritual|Q11675410|WD=Q11675410|1=narukama shinji}}, which predicts good or bad fortune by the sound of the kettle.<ref name="map" />

It is said that the local politician {{ill|lt=Tsuyoshi Inukai|Q354687|WD=Q354687|1=Inukai Tsuyoshi}} revered Kibitsu Shrine, believing that Inukai Ken-no-Mikoto, the distant ancestor of the Inukai family, was the deity of Okibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto.<ref name="map">{{Cite web|Japanese book|url=https://okayama-kanko.net/sightseeing/_cms/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/85ba4c00217acc9f333e2c349 6cdce52.pdf|title=Kibiji Tourist Map|publisher=Okayama Tourism and Convention Association|date=|accessdate=2025-01-13|pages=9-10}}</ref>. A bronze statue of Tsuyoshi Inukai was erected on the shore of Kamiike Pond, and the company name of Kibitsu Shrine was also written by Tsuyoshi Inukai.The Spring Festival is held on the second Sunday in May, and the Autumn Festival is held on the second Sunday in October. Among these, the Seventy-Five Zentai Ceremony, in which 75 tables are carried from the Gotoden through the corridor to the main shrine, is one of the three major festivals in Okayama Prefecture. 75 Zentai Shinto ritual|publisher=Okayama Prefecture Tourism Federation|date=|accessdate=2025-11-15|pages=}}</ref>.

"{{ill|lt=Plum|Q157763|WD=Q157763|1=Prunus mume}}", "{{ill|lt=Camellia|Q160121|WD=Q160121|1=Camellia japonica}}", "{{ill|lt=Sakura|Q871991|WD=Q871991|1=Cherry blossom}}", "{{ill|lt=Button (Plant)|Q163018|WD=Q163018|lt=Button|1=Paeonia × suffruticosa}}'', ``{{ill|lt=Azalea|Q189393|WD=Q189393|1=Rhododendron}}'', ``{{ill|lt=Satsuki|Q5366359|WD=Q5366359|1=Rhododendron indicum}}'', ``{{ill|lt=Hana iris|Q21558856|WD=Q21558856|1=Iris ensata var. ensata}}'', and ``{{ill|lt=Hydrangea|Q159219|WD=Q159219|1=Hydrangea macrophylla}}'', which are also famous flower spots<ref name="map" />. It is also known as a famous spot for {{ill|lt=autumn leaves|Q1156320|WD=Q1156320|1=Autumn leaf color}} in {{ill|lt=Ginkgo|Q43284|WD=Q43284|1=Ginkgo biloba}}.

=== History ===

=== Founding ===
[[File:Kibi's Nakayama (from Kibitsu Shrine).JPG|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Enshrined{{ill|lt=Kibi's Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}}}}{{small|On the far right is the pine trees on the approach. }}]]
According to the shrine's legend, the enshrined deity, Daikibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto, lived in a thatched shrine at the foot of {{ill|lt=Kibi Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}}, and was buried at the top of the mountain at the age of 281. Regarding the founding of Kibitsu Shrine, there is a theory that it was founded by {{ill|lt=Emperor Nintoku|Q313119|WD=Q313119|1=Emperor Nintoku}} to honor the achievements of Dai Kibitsuhiko no Mikoto, while a shrine legend says that it began when Kayaomi Narumi no Mikoto, the fifth-generation descendant, built a shrine in the thatched shrine and enshrined his life.<ref name="map" />

=== Outline ===
{{ill|lt=Imperial Court (Japan)|Q30253177|WD=Q30253177|lt=Imperial Court|1=Imperial Court of Japan}}, it was deeply revered, and in national history {{ill|lt=Jowa (Japan)|Q1075605|WD=Q1075605|lt=Jowa|1=Jōwa (Heian period)}} The first record is that he received the lower rank of Junior Fourth Rank (Junior Fourth Rank) in the year 14 ({{ill|lt=847|Q30354|WD=Q30354|1=847}}), and the following year he was promoted to the upper rank of Junior Fourth Rank (Junior Fourth Rank). In the second year of {{ill|lt=Ninju|Q1373077|WD=Q1373077|1=Ninju}} ({{ill|lt=852|Q30383|WD=Q30383|1=852}}), the divine rank was (Rank)|Q240268|Dignity}} Instead of Hon'i, he was given Shihon, and in {{ill|lt=10th century|Q8052|WD=Q8052|1=10th century}}, he was promoted to Ippon.

{{ill|lt=extension (era name)|Q1327274|WD=Q1327274|lt=Extended|1=Enchō}} "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" established in 5 years ({{ill|lt=927 years|Q30470|WD=Q30470|1=927}}) {{j alink|Engishiki Shinmeicho|Q11064932|Shinmeicho}}, {{ill|lt=Bichū|Q1047514|WD=Q1047514|1=Bitchū Province}}{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kayagun|1=UNKNOWN}} has "Kibitsuhiko Shrine <ref>{{ill|lt=Kogakukan University|Q1797584|WD=Q1797584|1=Kogakkan University}} Publishing Department, ``Shikinaisha Investigation Report Vol. 22 Sanyo Road'', listed as ``Meishin University'' and listed in {{ill|lt=Meishin Taisha|Q9610964|WD=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}}. </ref>.In the early {{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|WD=Q193292|1=Heian period}}, Kibitsu Shrine was given {{ill|lt=fūto|Q11458391|WD=Q11458391|1=Fūko}} by the imperial court, and the shrine area expanded by adding donated land, and eventually it was donated to the government and turned into a {{ill|lt=manor (Japan)|Q1887569|WD=Q1887569|lt=manor|1=Shōen}}<ref name="Early modern times">{{Cite journal |Japanese book |author= Hiroshi Shinomiya |title=Aspects of the Separation of Shinto and Buddhism at Kibitsu Shrine in Early Modern Times |journal= Rissho University Graduate School Annual Report |volume=39 |issue= |publisher=Rissho University Graduate School of Letters |date= |pages=33-48 |url=https://rissho.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/10438}}</ref>.

In the early {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|WD=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}}, it was donated to {{ill|lt=Ninnaji|Q1202871|WD=Q1202871|1=Ninna-ji}} and became its fief, but during the {{ill|lt=Nanbokucho period (Japan)|Q264012|WD=Q264012|lt=Nanbokucho period|1=Nanboku-chō period}}, control of Ninnaji Temple was threatened due to conflicts<ref name="Early modern" />. Furthermore, after the {{ill|lt=Onin War|Q385676|WD=Q385676|1=Ōnin War}}, shrine territory was sometimes controlled by the {{ill|lt=Hosokawa clan|Q2736120|WD=Q2736120|1=Hosokawa clan}}, the protector of Bicchu Province, and the Matsuda clan, a local power.<ref name="Early Modern Period" />At the end of the {{ill|lt=Sengoku period (Japan)|Q204023|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}, the power of the {{ill|lt=Mori clan|Q914637|WD=Q914637|1=Mōri clan}} came to power, and {{ill|lt=Muneharu Shimizu|Q1046032|WD=Q1046032|1=Shimizu Muneharu}} and others effectively ruled <ref name="Early modern" />. Furthermore, after the unification of the country by {{ill|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Q187550|WD=Q187550|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi}}, it became the territory of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hideie Ukita|1=UNKNOWN}} and received a donation of shrine territory<ref name="Early Modern Period" />. Furthermore, the ruling relationship with Ninna-ji Temple continued until the early modern period, and it was particularly influenced by rituals.In the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, it first came under the control of the Bicchu magistrate {{ill|lt=Masatsugu Kobori|Q11459515|WD=Q11459515|1=Kobori Masatsugu}} as a territory under the direct control of the {{ill|lt=Tokugawa clan|Q1412769|WD=Q1412769|1=Tokugawa clan}}, and then Miyauchi village, where Kibitsu Shrine is located, became the {{ill|lt=Niwase clan|Q3034514|WD=Q3034514|1=Niwase Domain}} territory.<ref name="Early modern" />. In April of Keicho 6 ({{ill|lt=1601|Q6725|WD=Q6725|1=1601}}), 160 koku were donated by {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|WD=Q171977|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, and after deducting the 60 koku of land removed from the precincts, the total was 100 koku, maintaining the stone height of the Ukita clan era<ref name="Early Modern" />. However, since the {{ill|lt=shuinjo|Q11093673|WD=Q11093673|1=shuinjō}} was simply written as ``Bicchu Imperial Palace Shinryo,'' there was a dispute between the shrine family and the shrine monks within the shrine over the destination<ref name="Early Modern Period" />. In the 3rd year of Kanbun ({{ill|lt=1663|Q7577|WD=Q7577|1=1663}}), the ruling of {{ill|lt=Temple and Shrine Bugyo|Q1036279|WD=Q1036279|1=Jisha-bugyō}} allowed shrine and family members to manage the main petition, and the red seals from 5th year of Kanbun ({{ill|lt=1665|Q7582|WD=Q7582|1=1665}}) clearly stated "Kibitsu Daimyo Shrine territory"<ref name="Early modern" />. Even after that, Buddhist facilities such as the {{ill|lt=three-storied pagoda|Q11357687|WD=Q11357687|1=Three-storied pagoda}} remained in the precincts, and monks continued to read sutras in front of the shrine<ref name="Early Modern Period" />.However, in the 14th year of Kyoho ({{ill|lt=1729|Q6952|WD=Q6952|1=1729}}), the shrine and family groups requested the temple magistrate to remove the three-storied pagoda, claiming that it was difficult to repair due to age-related deterioration and was dangerous in the event of wind, rain, or earthquakes, and the Buddhist side requested an injunction. The debate between the two leaders went beyond the pros and cons of removing the three-storied pagoda, to whether the shrine should be a syncretistic shrine of Shintoism and Buddhism, or whether the syncretism of Shintoism and Buddhism should be abolished as the only Shinto shrine.<ref name="Early Modern Period" /> The temple magistrate was the only one who did not directly judge whether it was Shinto or not, but it approved the removal of the three-storied pagoda, denied that the temple had anything to do with the shrine, and determined that the temple had no qualifications to sue. Buddhist buildings such as the three-storied pagoda have disappeared from maps of the precincts from the Kyoho period onward, and it is believed that the separation of Shinto and Buddhism was completed during this period.

After the {{ill|lt=Meiji Restoration|Q8707|WD=Q8707|1=Meiji Restoration}}, in {{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}4 ({{ill|lt=1871|Q7746|WD=Q7746|1=1871}}), it was ranked as {{ill|UNKNOWN|WD=Q134917280|lt=Kokuheichusha|1=Kokuhei Chūsha}} in the {{ill|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System|Q712534|WD=Q712534|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, and its official name was changed to the current ``Kibitsu Shrine''. In {{ill|lt=1914|Q2083|WD=Q2083|1=1914}} ({{ill|lt=Taisho|Q329174|WD=Q329174|1=Taishō era}}3), it was promoted to {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kanpei Chusha|1=UNKNOWN}}.

=== Precincts ===

=== Main shrine and worship hall ===
[[File:Kibitsu Jinja -01.jpg|thumb|400px|right|{{center|Main shrine and worship hall (national treasure)}}]]The existing main shrine and worship hall were built in the first year of {{ill|lt=Meitoku|Q1145032|WD=Q1145032|1=Meitoku}} of the {{ill|lt=Muromachi period|Q334845|WD=Q334845|1=Muromachi period}} ({{ill|lt=1390|Q6375|WD=Q6375|1=1390}}) under the orders of {{ill|lt=Emperor Gokogon|Q555465|WD=Q555465|1=Emperor Go-Kōgon}}.{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Muromachi Shogunate|1=UNKNOWN}}The third shogun Yoshimitsu Ashikaga|Q248381}} started construction and moved to {{ill|lt=Oei|Q1193078|WD=Q1193078|1=Ōei}} in 1425.<ref>[http://www.kibitujinja.com/about/honden.html Shrine official website], [http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=4 "Okayama's Cultural Properties"] (Okayama Prefecture website), [https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/195650 Cultural Heritage Online] etc. indicate that the main shrine was built in 1425 ({{ill|lt=1425|Q6283|WD=Q6283|1=1425}}). ``Weekly Asahi Encyclopedia Japan's National Treasures'' No. 29 (Asahi Shimbun, 1997) states that the main shrine was completed in the 12th year of Oei ({{ill|lt=1405|Q6124|WD=Q6124|1=1405}}), and that the temporary roof was replaced with cypress bark in the 32nd year of Oei, and the shrine was officially transferred to the shrine. </ref>. A gabled and flat worship hall is connected to the front of the main hall, which is built with a gabled gable structure. Hiyoku Irimoya-zukuri is a roof style in which two {{ill|lt=Irimoya-zukuri|Q855025|WD=Q855025|1=East Asian hip-and-gable roof}} roofs are arranged one behind the other, and is also called ``Kibitsu-zukuri.''The size of the main shrine is comparable to the main shrine of {{ill|lt=Izumo Taisha|Q696362|WD=Q696362|1=Izumo-taisha}} and {{ill|lt=Yasaka Shrine|Q692714|WD=Q692714|1=Yasaka Shrine}}, and the influence of Buddhist architecture can be seen everywhere. It is one step higher than the ground, and is built on a stucco-coated earthen platform (Kamebukuro), with a floor plan of 5 ken in the front, 7 ken in the back, and 8 ken in beam space, and the roof is {{ill|lt=cypress bark|Q90373477|WD=Q90373477|1=cypress bark roof}}. Inside, there is a closed inner hall in the center and an inner hall in front of it, surrounded by a lower middle hall, and in front of the middle hall is an even lower vermillion platform (Akenodan), which is surrounded by an even lower outer hall. In this way, it has a unique structure in which the floor height gradually increases from the outside to the inside. The upper half of the wall is surrounded by renji windows, which are rare for shrines. It is said to be the only example of {{ill|lt=Daibutsu-sama|Q3012037|WD=Q3012037|1=Daibutsuyō}} (daibutsuyo) applied to the main hall of a shrine, such as the shape of the inset wood, the bowl, and the rainbow beam.

The worship hall was built at the same time as the main shrine, with three girders (side lines) and one beam (front) with gables; the front is gabled and the back is connected to the main shrine. There are mokoshi floors on the front and sides. The roof is made of cypress bark like the main hall, but the lower floor is made of tile. These main shrines and worship halls are designated as {{ill|lt=National Treasure|Q1139795|WD=Q1139795|1=National Treasure (Japan)}}. - 283</ref><ref name="Main shrine and worship hall"/>.

=== Setsusha ===
[[File:Hongu Shrine (Kibitsu Shrine precinct shrine).JPG|right|thumb|200px|{{center|Hongu Shrine}}]]
It is said that in ancient times there were five shrine buildings and 72 subsidiary shrines. The five shrine buildings (Main Shrine, Hongu Shrine, Shingu Shrine, Naiku Shrine, and Iwayama Shrine) are collectively referred to as ``Kibitsu Gosho Daimyojin''. </ref>. {{ill|lt=2025|Q49616|WD=Q49616|1=2025}} ({{ill|lt=Reiwa|Q62609017|WD=Q62609017|1=Reiwa era}}7) Currently, Shingu Shrine and Naiku Shrine are enshrined in Hongu Shrine.
* Hongu Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: {{ill|lt=Emperor Korei|Q313041|WD=Q313041|1=Emperor Kōrei}} (7th generation. Father of Daikibitsuhiko no Mikoto).
** Shingu Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Kibi Takehiko no Mikoto (son of Wakahiko Kenkibitsu Hiko no Mikoto). Enshrined at Hongu Shrine. It was enshrined in Higashiyama in the south until the end of the Meiji period.
** Naiku Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Hyakuta Yumiya Hime no Mikoto (wife of Daikibitsuhiko no Mikoto). Enshrined at Hongu Shrine. It was originally enshrined on the mountain in the southern part of {{ill|lt=Kibi Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}}.
* Sanshagu - A collective term for the following three companies.
** Kasuga Shrine
** Daijingu Shrine
** Hachiman Shrine
* Iwayama Shrine - One of the Gosho Daimyojin shrines. Enshrined deity: Kenhikkatabetsu no Mikoto (landlord deity of Kibi Province).
* Taki Matsuri Shrine
* Ebisusha
*Soreisha Shrine
* Ichidosha
* Uga Shrine - Enshrined on the island of Kamiike.

=== Cultural assets ===

=== National Treasure ===
* Main shrine and worship hall (attached ridge plate [Meiwa 6], ridge plate [Koka 2]) (building)
*: {{ill|lt=Muromachi period|Q334845|WD=Q334845|1=Muromachi period}}[[wikt:Mid period|Middle period]], constructed in 1997 ({{ill|lt=1425|Q6283|WD=Q6283|1=1425}}). The main shrine and worship hall are designated as one building. {{ill|lt=1902|Q2043|WD=Q2043|1=1902}} ({{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}35th year) On April 17th, it was designated as a special protected building based on the {{ill|lt=Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|Q11411552|WD=Q11411552|1=Ancient Temples and Shrines Preservation Law}}. Designated as a national treasure on March 29, {{ill|lt=1952|Q5272|WD=Q5272|1=1952}} ({{ill|lt=Showa|Q327567|WD=Q327567|1=Shōwa era}}27) based on {{ill|lt=Cultural Properties Protection Law|Q1188502|WD=Q1188502|1=Cultural Properties Protection Law}}<ref name="Main shrine and worship hall">{{Nationally designated cultural properties database|102|2993|Kibitsu Shrine main shrine and worship hall}}<br />[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=4 Kibitsu Shrine main shrine and worship hall] {{ja icon}} (Okayama prefecture homepage "Okayama cultural assets"). </ref>.

=== Important cultural property (designated by the country) ===
* Minamizuishinmon (building)
*: Built in the 2nd year of Enbun ({{ill|lt=1357|Q6135|WD=Q6135|1=1357}}) during the Muromachi period [[wikt:first half|early]]. {{ill|lt=1911|Q2076|WD=Q2076|1=1911}} ({{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}44) Designated on April 17th<ref name="Minamizuishinmon">{{Nationally designated cultural property database|102|2994|Kibitsu Shrine Minamizuishinmon}}<br />[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=5 Kibitsu Shrine Minami Zuishinmon] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>.
* Hokuzuishinmon (building)
*: Built in the 12th year of Tenbun ({{ill|lt=1543|Q6523|WD=Q6523|1=1543}}) during the Muromachi period [[wikt:late|late]]. {{ill|lt=1913|Q2080|WD=Q2080|1=1913}} ({{ill|lt=Taisho|Q329174|WD=Q329174|1=Taishō era}}2) Designated on April 14th<ref name="Kitazuishinmon">{{National designated cultural property database|102|2995|Kibitsu Shrine Kitazuijinmon}}<br />[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=6 Kibitsu Shrine Kitazuishinmon] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>.
* Okamaden (building)*: Constructed in {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|WD=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, {{ill|lt=Keicho|Q1328185|WD=Q1328185|1=Keichō}}17 ({{ill|lt=1612|Q6771|WD=Q6771|1=1612}}). {{ill|lt=1980|Q2439|WD=Q2439|1=1980}} Designated on January 26, 1972<ref name="Okama-dono">{{Nationally designated cultural properties database|102|2996|Kibitsu Shrine Okama-dono}}<br />[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=7 Kibitsu Shrine Okamaden] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>.
* 1 pair of wooden lion guardian dogs (sculpture)
*: Created from the late {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|WD=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}} period to the Nanbokucho period. It is enshrined on the east and west sides of the inner hall of the main shrine. {{ill|lt=2002|Q1987|WD=Q1987|1=2002}} ({{ill|lt=Heisei|Q234510|WD=Q234510|1=Heisei era}}14) Designated on June 26th<ref>{{Nationally designated cultural properties database|201|10545|Wooden lion guardian dog}}<br />[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=518 Wooden lion guardian dog] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>.

=== Important intangible folk cultural property (designated by the country) ===
* {{ill|lt=Bicchu Kagura|Q11387313|WD=Q11387313|1=Bichu Kagura}}
*: Kagura dedicated throughout the Bitchu region, and performed at Kibitsu Shrine on the 10th of every month. The preservation organization is the Bitchu Kagura Preservation Society. Designated on February 3, 1979 icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage “Okayama Cultural Properties”). </ref>.

=== Okayama prefecture designated cultural property ===
* Important cultural property (tangible cultural property)
** Corridor (building) - Constructed during the Sengoku period and the Tensho era ({{ill|lt=1573|Q6678|WD=Q6678|1=1573}} - {{ill|lt=1591|Q6766|WD=Q6766|1=1591}}). {{ill|lt=1976|Q2480|WD=Q2480|1=1976}} Designated on March 27, 1976. </ref>.
** Odachi inscribed by Hideyuki Osafune (craft) - Muromachi period, Choroku 3 ({{ill|lt=1459|Q6524|WD=Q6524|1=1459}}). Deposited at Okayama Prefectural Museum. {{ill|lt=1982|Q2436|WD=Q2436|1=1982}} Designated on April 9, 1982 <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=700 Odachi, inscribed Bishū Osafune Hideyuki] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>. Blade length 127.2 cm, warp 3.9 cm. Kizukuri, hermitage building. Hideyuki is a representative figure among the {{ill|lt=Osafune school|Q11653605|WD=Q11653605|1=Osafune school}} branch of swordsmiths called the Kowarari school.** Odachi Norimitsu (craft) - Made in the Muromachi period, Bun'an 3 ({{ill|lt=1446|Q6430|WD=Q6430|1=1446}}). Deposited at {{ill|lt=Okayama Prefectural Museum|Q3247162|WD=Q3247162|1=Okayama Prefectural Museum}}. {{ill|lt=1994|Q2067|WD=Q2067|1=1994}} Designated on April 5, 1994 <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=701 Odachi Norimitsu] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>. Total length 377.3 cm, blade length 226.7 cm, warp 5 cm, weight 13 kg. Hog-zukuri, round building. The largest Japanese sword in Japan during the Koto period. Although there is no evidence that it was used as a votive sword, the entire blade is hardened, the {{ill|lt=stem (sword)|Q1963918|WD=Q1963918|lt=stem|1=nakago}} is long, and the three mekugi holes are evenly spaced, indicating that it was made with actual combat in mind.
** Gyodo mask (craft) - Deposited at Okayama Prefectural Museum. {{ill|lt=1959|Q5302|WD=Q5302|1=1959}} (Showa 34) Designated on March 27th <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=699 Gyodo-men] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>.** Goryeo version of All Sutras (calligraphs/scriptures) - Korean scriptures of {{ill|lt=Koryo|Q28208|WD=Q28208|1=Goryeo}}{{ill|lt=period|Q11514315|WD=Q11514315|1=Historical period}}. Designated on March 27, 1959 (Showa 34) <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=594 Goryeo version of all sutras] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>.
** Paper-backed sumi-sho renga (calligraphy/scripture) - A collection of haiku from the Horaku renga performed at Kibitsu Shrine in the 8th year of Oei ({{ill|lt=1401|Q6110|WD=Q6110|1=1401}}). Designated on March 27, 1959 (Showa 34) <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=764 Honsokusho Renga] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Cultural Properties of Okayama"). </ref>.
* Intangible folk cultural assets
** Imperial House Dance - Held on {{ill|lt=July 31st|Q2715|WD=Q2715|1=July 31}} in the Imperial Palace district of Monzen-cho. Designated on March 27, 1959. </ref>.

=== Damage ===
* {{ill|lt=2021|Q49628|WD=Q49628|1=2021}} ({{ill|lt=Reiwa|Q62609017|WD=Q62609017|1=Reiwa era}}3) From January 15th to 22nd, it was discovered that someone had made linear scratches on the pillars of the shrine's worship hall and corridor. In February of the same year, a suspect who had damaged {{ill|lt=Matsuyama Castle|Q981357|WD=Q981357|1=Matsuyama Castle (Iyo)}} and {{ill|lt=Kochi Castle|Q1012815|WD=Q1012815|1=Kōchi Castle}} was arrested for violating {{ill|lt=Cultural Properties Protection Act|Q1188502|WD=Q1188502|1=Cultural Properties Protection Law}}, and was arrested again for committing similar crimes at Kibitsu Shrine.<ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book|date=2021-02-13 |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210213122041/https://www.jiji.com/jc/article?k=2021021300375&g=soc |title=Rearrest of 47-year-old man suspected of damaging Kibitsu Shrine - Okayama Prefectural Police |website=Jiji Press|publisher=Jiji Press|accessdate=2021-02-13}} {{ja icon}}</ref>.

'''Surroundings'''
[[File:Nakayama Chausuyama Kofun, haisho.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|{{ill|lt=Nakayama Chausuyama Kofun|Q11364273|WD=Q11364273|1=Nakayama Chausuyama Kofun}}}}{{small|The Imperial Household Agency-regulated tomb of Daikibitsuhiko no Mikoto. }}]]* {{ill|lt=Nakayama of Kibi|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}}
*: Many ancient tombs and ancient ritual sites remain in Nakayama, Kibi, at the rear of the temple grounds, and it is believed that it was worshiped as {{ill|lt=Shintaiyama|Q1595289|WD=Q1595289|1=Sacred mountains}} since ancient times. At the summit of Mt. Chausu (160 meters) in the center, there is an ancient tomb believed to be the grave of Daikibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto, and at the summit of the highest peak, Mt. Ryuo (northern peak, 175 meters above sea level), there is {{ill|lt=Iwaza|Q11587880|WD=Q11587880|1=Iwakura rock}}, where Kibitsuhiko Shrine is enshrined.
** {{ill|lt=Nakayama Chausuyama Tumulus|Q11364273|WD=Q11364273|1=Nakayama Chausuyama Kofun}} ​​- {{ill|lt=keyhole-shaped tumulus|Q11268718|WD=Q11268718|1=Zenpōkōenfun}} with a length of 120 meters. It has been designated by the Imperial Household Agency as the ``Grave of Great Kibitsuhiko.''

Okayama Prefecture's designated historic site <ref>[http://www.pref.okayama.jp/cgi-bin/bunka/culture/controller/client/resultDetail.cgi?id=325 Dengayoujikan Ruins] {{ja icon}} (Okayama Prefecture homepage "Okayama Cultural Properties"). </ref>.

In ``{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|WD=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}'' it is listed as ``Kibitsuhiko Shrine.'' {{ill|lt=2025|Q49616|WD=Q49616|1=2025}} ({{ill|lt=Reiwa|Q62609017|WD=Q62609017|1=Reiwa era}}7) {{jalink|current|Q193168} }'s formal name is 'Kibitsu Shrine''' <ref>Currently, Bicchu and Bingo Ichinomiya call themselves ``Kibitsu Shrine,'' but only Bizen Ichinomiya calls itself ``Kibitsuhiko Shrine.'' </ref>.

=== Overview ===
It faces north at the northwest foot of {{ill|lt=Kibi no Nakayama|Q135646238|WD=Q135646238|1=Mount Kibi no Nakayama}} (175 meters above sea level) on the border between {{ill|lt=Bizen Province|Q1047514|WD=Q1047514|1=Bitchū Province}} in the western part of Okayama City. Nakayama in Kibi has been known as {{ill|lt=Shintaiyama|Q1595289|WD=Q1595289|1=Sacred mountains}} since ancient times, and Bizen Province Ichinomiya, {{ill|lt=Kibitsuhiko Shrine|Q500763|WD=Q500763|1=Kibitsuhiko Shrine}}, is enshrined at the northeastern foot of the mountain. Both our company and Kibitsuhiko Shrine enshrine {{ill|lt=Kibitsuhiko no Mikoto|Q65318|WD=Q65318|lt=Okibitsuhiko no Mikoto|1=Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto}}, who is said to have ruled the area, as the main deity, and the clan of life is enshrined here.

Originally, it was the general guardian of {{ill|lt=Kibikuni|Q1155128|WD=Q1155128|1=Kingdom of Kibi}}, but due to the division of Kibikuni into three kingdoms, it became the Ichinomiya of Bichoku, and its branch spirit is the Ichinomiya of Bizen and {{ill|lt=Bingokuni|Q1049113|WD=Q1049113|1=Bingo Province}} (Bizen: Kibitsuhiko Shrine, Bingo: {{ill|lt=Kibitsu Shrine) (Fukuyama City)|Q6404042|WD=Q6404042|lt=Kibitsu Shrine|1=Kibitsu Shrine (Bingo)}}). For this reason, Kibitsuhiko Shrine in Bizen takes the names of ``Kibisou Chinju'' and ``Sanbi Ichinomiya''. </ref>.The main shrine, which is said to have been built {{ill|lt=Yoshimitsu Ashikaga|Q248381|WD=Q248381|1=Ashikaga Yoshimitsu}}, is the only {{ill|lt=Hiyoku-irimoya-zukuri|Q3196321|WD=Q3196321|1=Kibitsu-zukuri}} (Kibitsu-zukuri) in Japan, and is designated as a {{ill|lt=national treasure|Q1139795|WD=Q1139795|1=National Treasure (Japan)}} along with the worship hall. Additionally, three shrine buildings have been designated as national {{ill|lt=Important Cultural Properties|Q1188622|WD=Q1188622|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}. It is also famous for {{ill|lt=Narukama Shinto ritual|Q11675410|WD=Q11675410|1=narukama shinji}}, which predicts good or bad fortune by the sound of the kettle.<ref name="map" />

It is said that the local politician {{ill|lt=Tsuyoshi Inukai|Q354687|WD=Q354687|1=Inukai Tsuyoshi}} revered Kibitsu Shrine, believing that Inukai Ken-no-Mikoto, the distant ancestor of the Inukai family, was the deity of Okibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto.<ref name="map">{{Cite web|Japanese book|url=https://okayama-kanko.net/sightseeing/_cms/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/85ba4c00217acc9f333e2c349 6cdce52.pdf|title=Kibiji Tourist Map|publisher=Okayama Tourism and Convention Association|date=|accessdate=2025-01-13|pages=9-10}}</ref>. A bronze statue of Tsuyoshi Inukai was erected on the shore of Kamiike Pond, and the company name of Kibitsu Shrine was also written by Tsuyoshi Inukai.The Spring Festival is held on the second Sunday in May, and the Autumn Festival is held on the second Sunday in October. Among these, the Seventy-Five Zentai Ceremony, in which 75 tables are carried from the Gotoden through the corridor to the main shrine, is one of the three major festivals in Okayama Prefecture. 75 Zentai Shinto ritual|publisher=Okayama Prefecture Tourism Federation|date=|accessdate=2025-11-15|pages=}}</ref>.

"{{ill|lt=Plum|Q157763|WD=Q157763|1=Prunus mume}}", "{{ill|lt=Camellia|Q160121|WD=Q160121|1=Camellia japonica}}", "{{ill|lt=Sakura|Q871991|WD=Q871991|1=Cherry blossom}}", "{{ill|lt=Button (Plant)|Q163018|WD=Q163018|lt=Button|1=Paeonia × suffruticosa}}'', ``{{ill|lt=Azalea|Q189393|WD=Q189393|1=Rhododendron}}'', ``{{ill|lt=Satsuki|Q5366359|WD=Q5366359|1=Rhododendron indicum}}'', ``{{ill|lt=Hana iris|Q21558856|WD=Q21558856|1=Iris ensata var. ensata}}'', and ``{{ill|lt=Hydrangea|Q159219|WD=Q159219|1=Hydrangea macrophylla}}'', which are also famous flower spots<ref name="map" />. It is also known as a famous spot for {{ill|lt=autumn leaves|Q1156320|WD=Q1156320|1=Autumn leaf color}} in {{ill|lt=Ginkgo|Q43284|WD=Q43284|1=Ginkgo biloba}}.

=== Enshrined God ===
The following nine deities are enshrined.
; Main enshrined deity
:* {{ill|lt=Kibitsuhiko no Mikoto|Q65318|WD=Q65318|lt=Okibitsuhiko no Mikoto|1=Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto}} (Ookibitsuhiko no Mikoto)
:*: He was the third {{ill|lt=prince|Q12886381|WD=Q12886381|1=Imperial Prince}} of the 7th {{ill|lt=Emperor Korei|Q313041|WD=Q313041|1=Emperor Kōrei}}, and his original name was ``Hiko Isaserihiko no Mikoto (Isosa Serihiko no Mikoto). {{ill|lt=Emperor Sujin|Q333530|WD=Q333530|1=Emperor Sujin}} In 10 years, he was dispatched to Sanyo Province as one of the Shoguns of the Four Paths, and subdued Kibi with his younger brother Wakahiko Takekibitsuhiko no Mikoto. It is said that his descendants became {{ill|lt=Kunizo|Q2483673|WD=Q2483673|1=Kuni no miyatsuko}} of Kibi, and became {{ill|lt=Kibi clan|Q11412645|WD=Q11412645|lt=Kibi vassal|1=Kibi clan}} of {{ill|lt=ancient|Q41493|WD=Q41493|1=Ancient history}}{{ill|lt=gozoku|Q84066|WD=Q84066|1=Gōzoku}}.

In ancient times, it was known as ``Kibitsu Gosho Daimyojin,'' which consisted of five shrines, the main shrine and four other shrines.
